newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore PM aims for clean sweep at election.
newsitem.headline: Singapore PM aims for clean sweep at election.

text.p: Singaporeans voted in a general election on Thursday with the ruling party seeking to maintain its overwhelming dominance of parliament.
Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's People's Action Party (PAP) was already assured of a majority in the 83 member-parliament because the opposition was contesting only 36 seats.
But Goh, who leads a party which faced no opposition MPs for 13 years until 1981, sees losing even one seat as a defeat and has staked his prestige on keeping opposition representation at a minimum.
Before parliament was dissolved for the elections, opposition parties held just four seats of the then 81 total. Redrawn constituencies enlarge the next parliament by two seats.
Goh, who was returned unopposed in his own seat on December 23, visited a key constituency, Cheng San, to greet voters when polls opened at 8 a.m. (0000 GMT) on Thursday.

Cheng San, a multi-member constituency which elects five MPs in a winner-takes-all contest, has seen a strong challenge from the opposition Workers' Party (WP) and fierce attacks by the PAP on a WP candidate, Tang Liang Hong.

Political analysts say defeat for the PAP in Cheng San, where some predict a close result, could damage Goh's reputation as a strong leader capable of winning elections. The last election was in 1991.

The PAP has led Singapore since 1959, transforming the island through strict central control into a prosperous city where the average per capita income is higher than in Britain, the old colonial power.
But opposition parties say they want alternative voices in parliament and a check on the PAP's dominance.
Goh said he was confident of victory in Cheng San but he and his deputies had staked their reputation on winning there.
Goh repeated criticism of Tang, whom he has called a "Chinese chauvinist", saying he endangered Singapore's multi-racial society, which is 77 percent Chinese but has minorities of Malays and Indians.
Race is an emotive issue in the city-state which saw several days of bloody riots in 1964, before its separation in 1965 from its northern neighbour Malaysia.
Goh and other PAP politicians have said they will sue Tang for defamation after the election for calling them "liars".
WP leader Joshua Jeyaretnam said on Wednesday Tang would sue Goh and had made a complaint to police alleging defamation.
Goh has used a multi-billion dollar programme to upgrade public housing to emphasise his party's ability in economic management and to lure voters away from the opposition.
Areas that return opposition MPs would miss out on the programme and become slums in 20 to 30 years' time, he said.
Goh on Thursday rejected complaints that allocating money for housing renovation on the basis of votes cast was unfair.
"You cannot upgrade all estates together," he said. "Surely in a war, when you have to ration food, you give to your own soldiers first, you don't give to the other side."

The foreign ministry last week described as "undisguised interference in Singapore's domestic politics" a comment by a U.S. State Department official criticising the tactic of linking votes with funds for housing projects.
A 60-year old Singaporean leaving a polling station in the north of Singapore on Thursday said he disapproved of linking upgrading to votes but would still vote for the PAP.
"For all my grouses, I cannot cut off my nose to spite my face. I will vote for the PAP," he told Reuters.
But another said what he called "the government's high-handedness" meant he would support the opposition.
Polls close at 8 p.m. (1200 GMT) and results were not expected until after midnight (1600 GMT). About 765,000 voters were due to vote in the contested seats. Voting is compulsory.
